concepts.name: Imagine-instruction paradigm
concepts.summary: A three-way comparison in which a stimulus with one property is presented neutrally, presented under an instruction to imagine it has a different property, and set against a matched stimulus that genuinely has that other property.
concepts.explanation: The paradigm exists to separate two readings of a modulation result. If the instruction "Imagine that the following code is written in Python" caused the model to re-encode a JavaScript snippet as Python throughout its activations, then python appearing in the J-lens would say nothing about the workspace specifically. Four stimulus categories are built: a JavaScript snippet against real Python, a present-tense sentence against a real past-tense one, a noun against a real verb, and a lowercase word against a real all-caps one, with 24 stimuli per category. Each is measured under a neutral instruction, under the imagine instruction, and in its matched-real form, at the stimulus token positions across the workspace layer range. The imagine instruction raises the property's name in the J-lens by several standard deviations while leaving the [[j-orthogonalized-property-probe|J-orthogonalized property probe]] within roughly one standard deviation of baseline; the real stimulus moves the probe by three to six.

concepts.name: Reverse dissociation (probe up, label absent)
concepts.summary: The second half of the dissociation: for some categories a real stimulus drives the property probe strongly while the property's name stays out of the J-lens entirely.
concepts.explanation: The forward direction shows an instruction moving the J-space without moving the underlying representation. The reverse shows the underlying representation moving without the J-space. A genuinely past-tense sentence drives the tense probe up six standard deviations, yet past remains far down the lens ranking. The paper reads the pair together as evidence that the two measures are independent, and that a property can be represented and used by the model without its label entering the workspace. The effect is reported for some but not all of the four categories.

concepts.name: Scoring a modulation trial
concepts.summary: The rule that decides whether a single modulation trial counts as a hit, which differs between the two concept-style task families and the line-width task.
concepts.explanation: For the category-instance and math-expression families, a trial is positive if the target reaches J-lens top-1 at any (layer, position) in the response - a single hit anywhere in the layer-by-position grid is enough, so the reported quantity is a fraction of trials. The line-width panels are scored differently, as precision: the fraction of top-1 numeric readouts that match the true width. The two panels therefore do not share a y-axis, and a rate from one is not comparable with a rate from the other. In the concurrent-task experiment the threshold is loosened from top-1 to rank 5 or better.

concepts.name: No-instruction baseline
concepts.summary: A control condition in which the target concept is never mentioned in the prompt, whose rate is approximately zero across all task families.
concepts.explanation: Without it, a target appearing in the lens could be an artifact of the prompt context rather than a response to the instruction. The measured baseline rate is approximately zero in every condition, which the paper takes as confirmation that the surrounding context alone does not place the target in J-lens readouts. It is also what makes the [[white-bear-effect|white bear effect]] statable: the ignore instruction produces target activation well below the focus instruction but clearly above zero, so the instruction to suppress is itself doing the activating. Note that this baseline is distinct from the mention condition, which does name the target and produces a substantial rate.

concepts.name: Phrasing spread within a condition
concepts.summary: Each instruction condition is instantiated with five to eight different wordings, and the per-wording rates are plotted individually rather than only as a condition mean.
concepts.explanation: A condition such as focus is not a single prompt but a family of them, and the main-text figures average over the family. The appendix figure plots each wording as its own dot with the condition mean as a bar, so the spread within a condition is visible alongside the gap between conditions. The spread is largest on the line-width task, where focus phrasings range from a direct "count the characters" to the more oblique "figure out the column number" and precision on Opus 4.5 runs from 14% to 56% across them. The paper attributes this partly to the task being harder to specify than the other two, and treats the phrasing sensitivity as a limit on how well the models control their own workspace contents.

concepts.name: Modulation and model size
concepts.summary: Under a focus instruction, the rate at which the target reaches the J-lens tends to rise with model size; the paper states this as a tendency rather than a measured scaling law.
concepts.explanation: The systematic modulation figure breaks results out by model as well as by task family and instruction condition. Under "think about X", the target appears in the lens on a substantial fraction of trials, and the paper says this tends to increase with model size. The claim is hedged and rests on a small set of models from one family rather than a fitted trend, and the line-width task does not follow the pattern of the other two on any condition. The suppression side of the comparison is not reported as scaling: the ignore condition suppresses the target below the mention rate on every model.

concepts.name: Shuffled partner control
concepts.summary: The baseline against which co-occupancy is read: the partner task's presence at a token is taken from a different prompt, one where that task was given on its own.
concepts.explanation: Raw co-occupancy is not interpretable on its own, because both tasks appear at the same rough density across the response and would overlap somewhat by chance. The control breaks any real interaction while keeping each task's marginal occupancy pattern: task A's tokens come from the dual-task prompt, task B's from a single-task prompt. The comparison is what turns the numbers into a claim. Two held concepts co-occupy at 0.46 against a control rate of 0.53, which the paper reads as the two ignoring each other; a concept and a computed answer co-occupy at 0.09 against 0.29, which it reads as active exclusion. Measurements are taken over layers 67 to 92.

concepts.name: Cost of holding two covert tasks
concepts.summary: A separate measurement from token-level sharing: how often each task's content still reaches the top of the lens anywhere in the response when the two are given together rather than alone.
concepts.explanation: Token-level exclusion could mean either that one task crowds the other out of the workspace or only that they take turns. The response-level measure separates these. Each task's content is scored as present if it reaches J-lens rank 5 or better at any token, alone versus paired. The rates under dual load stay close to the single-task rates, with the largest decline being the computed arithmetic answer at 95% to 72%. The paper's reading is that holding two concepts at once is essentially free, and that where there is a cost it falls on the ongoing computation rather than on the static concept it displaces.
